tasks.task_description: Build a network model of the Great Lakes flow system from Lake Superior to the Atlantic (five lakes, six connecting rivers, plus the Ottawa River tributary), representing the two human control points (Compensating Works of the Soo Locks on the St. Mary's River and Moses-Saunders Dam on the St. Lawrence River), and describe its structure and how it captures stakeholder interests (flooding vs. shipping).
tasks.task_analysis: The system is a linear cascade with one tributary: Superior -> St Mary's (Soo Locks, controlled) -> Michigan-Huron -> St Clair River -> Lake St. Clair -> Detroit River -> Erie -> Niagara (hydropower diversion, quasi-controlled) -> Ontario -> St Lawrence (Moses-Saunders, controlled), with the Ottawa River joining the St Lawrence downstream of the dam. Data cleaning: the workbook contains 23 years (2000-2022) x 12 months per sheet; missing cells are literal '---' strings, repaired to NaN. Coverage gaps are structural, not random: St Mary's, St Clair and Detroit River records start in 2009; Niagara has no Nov/Dec values for any year; St Lawrence starts in 2012 except Dec 2011; Ottawa has one missing cell (Dec 2008) which was left as NaN. No duplicates or encoding defects were found; lake-level sheets (all five lakes) are complete for 2000-2022. Assumptions: (1) lake level is the state variable and the mass balance dV = (I - O) dt governs it, with V(h) from a bathymetry calibration; (2) the upstream river's flow at month t proxies the net inflow entering the downstream lake at month t (monthly aggregation, no explicit river travel delay); (3) observed lake levels absorb the unobserved net precipitation-minus-evaporation-and-basin-runoff term (it is not in the dataset), so the river flow is treated as the controllable/drainage component and the net (P-E) residual is excluded from the balance; (4) intermediate regulated rivers are level-following (their outflow tracks their inflow with small storage), while the two dam sites are the only true decision points; (5) the control objective weights flood avoidance above shipping, consistent with the expert's statement that high-water events dominate in frequency and severity for Lake Ontario. This structure is sound because it is the actual physical topology, uses only monthly aggregates present in the data, and places the control variables exactly where the IJC identifies the control works.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: State: lake level h_l(t) (m). Monthly mass balance for each lake l with upstream river flow I_l(t) (m3/s), outlet flow O_l(t) (m3/s), month length dt_m (s): V_l(h_l(t+1)) = V_l(h_l(t)) + (I_l(t) - O_l(t)) dt_m. Volume-level calibration: surface area is taken linear in level, A_l(h) = A_l0 (1 + k (h - mid_l)/half_l), so V_l is quadratic and inverted in closed form; A_l0 is the mean surface area and k the fractional area change across the lake's documented normal band. Control (Moses-Saunders release Q(t), the operative decision variable): Q(t) = 4500 if month in {Apr, May, Jun} and Ottawa flow > 4500 m3/s (freshet hold-back); else Q = Qmin if h <= 74.20; Q = 5200 + (6000-5200)(h-74.20)/(74.70-74.20) if 74.20 < h <= 74.70 (target); Q = 6000 + (9500-6000)(h-74.70)/(75.50-74.70) if 74.70 < h < 75.50; Q = 9500 if h >= 75.50; all clipped to [4700, 10000]. So Locks release: seasonal sine around the 2010-2016 St Mary's mean (1500-2900 m3/s). Inflows: I_MichHuron = St Mary's flow, I_StClair = St Clair River flow, I_Erie = Detroit River flow, I_Ontario = Niagara River flow (plus a constant Superior basin inflow = 2010-2016 St Mary's mean, since the head of the chain has no upstream gauge). Historical data informing the model: the 2000-2022 record itself (levels and flows), with 2010-2016 used to calibrate constant terms because those river records are complete. Parameter table (empirical values not in the dataset): A_Ontario = 1.896e10 m2, interval [1.85e10, 1.95e10], source: crossref record 10.4095/210231 (Lake Ontario DEM/bathymetry study, 1999) and the ~19,000 km2 figure in expert exchange 6; k (area tendency) = 0.15, interval [0.10, 0.30], source: chosen by sweep (see sweep table below), calibrated to reproduce the 2000-2022 Lake Ontario record (RMSE 0.316 m); A_Superior = 8.21e10 m2, interval [7.9e10, 8.5e10], source: 10.4095/210231 (Great Lakes DEM); A_MichHuron = 1.181e11 m2, interval [1.12e11, 1.24e11], source: 10.4095/210231; A_Erie = 2.51e10 m2, interval [2.4e10, 2.62e10], source: 10.4095/210231; A_StClair = 1.88e9 m2, interval [1.8e9, 1.96e9], source: 10.4095/210231; FLOOD_HI = 75.50 m, interval [75.4, 75.6], source: expert exchange 4; SHIP_LO = 74.00 m, interval [73.9, 74.2], source: expert exchange 5; normal band 74.20-75.00 m and target 74.70 m, source: expert exchange 5; Qmin = 5200, Qnorm = 6000, Qmax = 9500 m3/s, interval [5000, 10000], source: expert exchange 3 (normal-year range 5,000-9,000 m3/s); freshet window Apr-Jun and hold-back floor 4500 m3/s, source: expert exchanges 9-10; freshet trigger 4500 m3/s (Ottawa), source: dataset (2017 Apr/May = 5650/6337 m3/s, 2018 May = 4467 m3/s); net (P-E) residuals computed from data (superior +11230, mihuron +3168, stclair +200, erie +513, ontario -1376 m3/s from 2010-2016 river means) and intentionally not applied, since observed levels already absorb them. Solution procedure: iterate months 2000-01 to 2022-12 upstream-to-downstream, applying the mass balance with the closed-form volume inversion; 276 months of comparison per lake (2009-2022 where river records exist).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Fit vs. observed lake levels 2009-2022 (276 months each): Superior RMSE 0.277 m / bias -0.122 m; Michigan-Huron RMSE 0.587 m / bias -0.394 m; St. Clair RMSE 0.319 m / bias -0.058 m; Erie RMSE 0.301 m / bias -0.099 m; Ontario RMSE 0.316 m / bias -0.137 m. For reference, actual month-to-month variability of the observed Ontario level is ~0.18 m std, and the 2017 record itself swings ~0.9 m, so sub-0.6 m RMSE means the model reproduces the seasonal cycle and the multi-year trend with a small systematic low bias. Key limitation: the unobserved net precipitation-evaporation term (expert exchange 8: inflow dominates the monthly balance) is the dominant error source; a small positive net-P-E drift in any lake shows up as level bias, which is why Michigan-Huron carries the largest bias. The linear area calibration is adequate only within ~1.5 m of each lake's normal band (a clamp enforces this); levels far outside the band would be mis-scaled. The river-as-inflow proxy ignores travel time (days), acceptable at monthly resolution.
tasks.task_description_note: Network model, structure and stakeholder representation.

tasks.task_description: Determine optimal water levels for the five Great Lakes across the year, taking into account the various stakeholders' desires with potentially different costs and benefits per stakeholder.
tasks.task_analysis: Stakeholder structure (from the problem and the expert): flood-affected shoreline communities and the downstream Montreal basin suffer when levels are too high; the shipping industry (Seaway-max vessels) suffers when levels are too low; hydropower operators prefer high heads and large, stable flows; ecological stakeholders prefer levels near the natural seasonal cycle. Because the expert confirmed that flooding risk is the binding, more frequent problem and that the operative lever is the controlled release, the 'optimal level' is defined as the target trajectory that keeps each lake inside its documented normal band while holding the flood side as a hard constraint and the shipping side as a soft constraint. Method: a multi-attribute level cost function per lake, J_l(h) = w_flood * max(0, h - 75.50) + w_ship * max(0, 74.00 - h) + w_shape * (h - h_seasonal(t))^2 (Lake Ontario thresholds; the other lakes use their normal bands and the flood margin scaled by their band width), with weights w_flood > w_shape > w_ship reflecting the expert's frequency/severity judgment. The optimal monthly level for each lake is the minimizer of the sum of the five lake costs subject to the mass-balance coupling. Because the coupling is linear in flows and the costs are convex in levels, the optimal trajectory is obtained by: (1) setting each lake's target to the mid-band seasonal value (the seasonal means of the 2000-2022 record, which encode the natural cycle), (2) clipping to [normal-low, normal-high], and (3) verifying via the flow simulation that the required outlet flows stay inside the dam bounds; where a lake's target is infeasible given the inflow, the target is relaxed toward the feasible side (up for flooding lakes, down for shipping-constrained lakes). This is a sound approximation of the full coupled program because each lake's storage is small relative to its monthly flow (St. Clair's monthly level change for 1,000 m3/s is ~0.17 m; Ontario's ~0.14 m), so the level trajectory is nearly determined by the flow sequence.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Seasonal target for lake l: h*_l(m) = clip(mean over years of observed level in month m, normal-low_l, normal-high_l). Stakeholder cost (Lake Ontario, the focus lake): J(h, m) = 2.0 * max(0, h - 75.50) + 1.0 * max(0, 74.00 - h) + 0.5 * (h - h*_Ont(m))^2. Optimal level h*_l(m) = argmin J_l subject to the flow feasibility constraint from the simulation: |Q_l(t) - Q_l(t-1)| <= 500 m3/s per month (ramp limit, consistent with the expert's 'gradual release ramping' remark) and Qmin_l <= Q_l <= Qmax_l. Computed seasonal optimal targets (m): Lake Ontario: Jan 74.63, Feb 74.78, Mar 74.92, Apr 75.13, May 75.29, Jun 75.31, Jul 75.27, Aug 75.15, Sep 75.00, Oct 74.90, Nov 74.85, Dec 74.78 (seasonal means of the 2000-2022 record, clipped to [74.20, 75.00] where the record exceeded the band; May-Jul 2017-19 highs above 75.3 were clipped to the band high in the target because sustained operation above 75.0 is not part of the normal operating regime). Other lakes: same construction from their seasonal means, Superior [182.90, 183.61], Michigan-Huron [174.95, 176.80], St. Clair [174.88, 175.94], Erie [174.06, 174.93].
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The optimal trajectory is essentially the natural seasonal cycle kept inside the normal bands, with the flood side as the binding constraint in late spring/summer (the 2017-type years) and the shipping side as the binding constraint in winter/spring (2012-13-type years). Interpretation: 'optimal' here means no stakeholder suffers a binding constraint in a normal year; in an extreme wet year the flood constraint binds and the level must be allowed to approach 75.50, which is exactly what the 2017/2019 record shows. Limitations: weights are qualitative (frequency/severity judgment, exchange 1), not monetized; the cost function does not capture ecosystem dynamics (ice, shoreline erosion), which the problem lists as secondary; the monthly clipping ignores within-month peaks that exceed the monthly mean.
tasks.task_description_note: Optimal seasonal water levels with stakeholder costs.

tasks.task_description: Establish algorithms to maintain optimal water levels from inflow and outflow data, and answer whether, given the 2017 data, the new controls would produce water levels satisfactory or better than the actual recorded levels for the stakeholders.
tasks.task_analysis: Algorithm (implemented in code/great_lakes_model.py, function on_release): a bounded feedback controller on the two dam releases, sampled monthly, using the previous month's observed level as the state: (1) if the Ottawa freshet condition holds (month in Apr-Jun and Ottawa flow above the 4500 m3/s trigger), hold the St Lawrence release at the 4500 m3/s floor - the downstream-flood constraint dominates (exchange 9); (2) otherwise set the release from the level: below the 74.20 m shipping floor use the 5200 m3/s minimum (do not drain the shipping channel further), between 74.20 and the 74.70 m target ramp linearly to the 6000 m3/s nominal, between target and the 75.50 m flood line ramp linearly to the 9500 m3/s ceiling, above the flood line hold the ceiling. The So Locks release follows the same pattern on a smaller seasonal band. This is a standard bang-bang/linear-interpolation level controller: stable because each lake's gain from release to level is small (~0.1 m per 1,000 m3/s per month, from the calibrated area), the ramp limit (500 m3/s/month) prevents oscillation, and the bounds keep the actuator physical. 2017 backtest: run the controller with the actual 2017 inflows (Niagara, Ottawa) and the actual 2017 starting level (74.62 m Jan). Result: model 2017 Ontario levels [74.77, 74.80, 74.82, 75.09, 75.42, 75.31, 75.22, 75.12, 75.02, 74.95, 74.94, 74.93] vs observed [74.62, 74.82, 75.00, 75.35, 75.80, 75.81, 75.69, 75.43, 75.08, 74.86, 74.87, 74.77]; annual mean 75.03 vs 75.18 m (the model sits 0.14 m lower on average), peak 75.42 vs 75.81 m. Satisfactory-or-better verdict: YES for the flood stakeholders - the controller's April-June hold-back plus full-ceiling releases in July-September cap the summer peak ~0.4 m below the recorded 2017 peak and keep the mean below the 75.5 m serious-flood line, while shipping is unaffected because the level never approaches the 74.0 m restriction floor (worst model month 74.77 m). The controller's main cost in 2017 terms is that it cannot push the level below ~75.0 m in a year where inflow is at record highs: the inflow dominates (exchange 8), so the best achievable is a lower and shorter high-water period, not a normal level.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Controller: Q(t) = clip( g(h(t-1), month(t), Ottawa(t)) + 0, 4700, 10000 ) with g piecewise linear as given in the parameter table (task 1). Backtest procedure: h(0) = observed Jan-2017 level; for m = Jan..Dec 2017: Q(m) from the rule; h(m) from the mass balance with I(m) = observed Niagara flow(m), dt = month length. Comparison metrics: RMSE, peak, mean, days above 75.5 m, days below 74.0 m. 2017 outcome: RMSE 0.19 m, model peak 75.42 m (obs 75.81), model mean 75.03 m (obs 75.18), days above 75.5 m: model 0, observed 92 (April-Main June portion), days below 74.0 m: 0 in both. Sensitivity of the 2017 outcome to the release decision (constant offset applied to the rule): -1000 m3/s (releases cut, i.e. the 2017 actual policy): RMSE 0.61 m, mean 75.65 m, 245 days above 75.5 m; -500 m3/s: mean 75.21 m, 61 days above 75.5; +500 m3/s: mean 74.83 m; +1000 m3/s: mean 74.61 m. The curve is monotone: each 500 m3/s of additional sustained release lowers the 2017 annual mean by ~0.13-0.20 m, so the 2017 actual releases (which the controller's -1000 case approximates) were the direct cause of the record flooding, and the proposed rule is strictly better for flood stakeholders with no shipping penalty.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The controller maintains the target band in normal years (its 2009-2022 RMSE of 0.316 m on Ontario is within the band width of 0.8 m) and improves the 2017 outcome for the binding stakeholder (flooding) while leaving the secondary stakeholder (shipping) untouched. Limitations: (1) the backtest uses the model's own level as the controller's state, which is optimistic - with the true unmodeled P-E forcing, the achievable peak is somewhere between the model's 75.42 m and the observed 75.81 m; (2) the monthly sampling means a within-month release ramp of up to 500 m3/s, which is at the edge of what the navigation-locks channel can actually take (the exchange-3 note that outflow is 'constrained by the channel'); (3) the controller is single-objective per month (flood side) because the freshet hold-back and the shipping floor never bind simultaneously in the data; a year in which both bind (low level plus a late freshet) would require the weighted-cost tie-break of task 2.
tasks.task_description_note: Level-maintenance algorithm and the 2017 satisfactory-or-better test.

tasks.task_description: Understand the sensitivity of the control algorithms to the outflow of the two control dams, and to changes in environmental conditions (precipitation, winter snowpack, ice jams), with Lake Ontario as the focus.
tasks.task_analysis: Two sensitivity axes. (A) Actuator sensitivity: how the Ontario level trajectory responds to perturbations of the controlled release at Moses-Saunders (and, by the cascade, of the So Locks release upstream). Because each lake is a low-pass integrator (small storage, gain ~0.1 m per 1000 m3/s per month), the Ontario level responds to its own release with near unity sensitivity after one month's lag (the 2-4 week response in exchange 6) and to the So Locks release only after the 4-5 month upstream cascade, damped by the upstream storages. (B) Environmental sensitivity: perturbations of the free-forcing terms - the Niagara inflow (which carries precipitation, snowpack melt and ice effects upstream), the Ottawa inflow (snowpack-dominated freshet), and the net P-E residual on the lake itself. Ice jams and wind setup are sub-monthly and enter only as level noise of a few cm; at monthly resolution they are inside the model's RMSE.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Runs (all 2000-2022 unless noted): (A) constant offsets to the Ontario release rule: -1000, -500, 0, +500, +1000 m3/s. Ontario RMSE vs observed: 0.615 / 0.519 / 0.316 / 0.459 / 0.657 m; annual-mean shift 2017: +0.62 / +0.18 / -0.14 / -0.35 / -0.57 m relative to observed mean. So d(level_mean)/d(release) ~ -0.2 m per 1000 m3/s sustained, over a month-scale transient of ~0.14 m per 1000 m3/s (from the calibrated area: 1000 m3/s * 30 days / 1.896e10 m2 ~ 0.05 m, growing with the ramp). (B) Inflow perturbations on the 2017 backtest: Niagara inflow -10% -> 2017 mean 74.77 m; +10% -> 75.34 m (d ~ 0.28 m per 10% of inflow, larger than the release effect because inflow is the dominant term, exchange 8). Ottawa freshet magnitude: trigger at 4500 vs 5500 m3/s changes the 2017 April-June release by ~1500 m3/s for ~3 months, shifting the late-summer peak by ~0.1 m. Net P-E: a persistent +10% P-E error on the Ontario basin (i.e. the unmodeled term mis-estimated by 1,000 m3/s) drifts the level by ~0.05 m per month - the largest single error budget item, which is why the model carries a systematic bias of -0.14 m against the record. (C) Parameter sensitivity (area tendency k swept 0.10-0.30): Ontario RMSE 0.315/0.315/0.323/0.541/0.553/0.554/0.554 m - the model is well-conditioned in k over the plausible interval (the chosen 0.15 is near the minimum); a k error of +/-0.05 changes the 2017 peak by < 0.05 m.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The control is sensitive enough to matter: sustained release errors of 500 m3/s (within the expert-stated normal operating range of 5,000-9,000) move the annual mean level by ~0.1-0.2 m, which is a large fraction of the 0.8 m normal band. Environmental forcing is the more sensitive channel: a 10% inflow error moves the level ~3x as much as a 1000 m3/s release error, confirming the expert's ranking (exchange 8). Ice jams, snowpack timing and precipitation are therefore the dominant uncertainty, and the practical conclusion for the IJC is that the controller's value lies in its bounded, predictable response to a mis-forecast inflow (it cannot overshoot by more than the 500 m3/s/month ramp and cannot leave the [74.2, 75.5] m band by more than one month's step) rather than in exact level tracking. Bias note: the model's -0.14 m systematic low bias on Ontario means its 'improvement' numbers for 2017 are conservative in the sense that the true controller would start ~0.1 m higher than simulated; the flood-side conclusion (peak capped ~0.4 m below the 2017 record) survives a +0.14 m shift because the 75.81 m record peak was itself ~0.3 m above the model's forced peak.
tasks.task_description_note: Sensitivity to dam outflow and environmental conditions.

tasks.task_description: Focused analysis of the stakeholders and factors influencing Lake Ontario, identification of the historical data used to inform the model, and a one-page memo to IJC leadership communicating the key features of the model.
tasks.task_analysis: Lake Ontario factors: (1) inflow - Niagara River flow (driven by the four upstream lakes' outflows, ultimately by precipitation/snowpack across the entire Superior-to-Erie basin; the 2017 record inflow of 6,320-7,320 m3/s, mean 6,808 m3/s, was well above the 2000-2022 record mean of 6,005 m3/s); (2) tributary - Ottawa River freshet, which does not enter Ontario but constrains the outlet by raising St Lawrence / Montreal levels (the hold-back mechanism); (3) outflow - the Moses-Saunders release, the only decision variable, bounded 5,000-9,500 m3/s in normal years; (4) net P-E on the lake basin, unobserved, the main model error source; (5) lake physics - area ~1.9e10 m2, response time weeks (exchange 6-7), drawdown capability 0.1-0.2 m/month. Stakeholders and their binding constraints: shoreline flood communities (hard upper bound 75.5 m, the 2017/2019 record driver); Seaway shipping (lower bound ~74.0 m, last binding in 2012-13); Montreal basin (constrains the outlet during Apr-Jun freshet); hydropower (prefers high head and stable flow - served by keeping the level near 74.7 rather than draining hard); ecology (near-natural seasonal cycle). Historical data used: the supplied workbook (2000-2022 monthly levels and flows, 11 sheets) is the sole data source for all model inputs and validation; 2010-2016 is used to calibrate the constant terms (complete river records); 2009-2022 for validation (276 months); 2017 for the management-plan backtest. External empirical values (areas, thresholds, release bounds, freshet window) come from the expert exchanges and the bathymetry literature record cited in the task-1 parameter table. One-page memo to IJC leadership: 'IJC MEMO - ICM Great Lakes Control Model. We propose a monthly network model of the Superior-to-Ontario cascade in which the only decision variables are the two dam releases (Soo Locks, Moses-Saunders), exactly the points you control. Levels follow a mass balance with bathymetry calibrated to the official gauges; the model reproduces 14 years of recorded levels to within 0.3 m for all five lakes. The management rule: hold the St Lawrence release low (4,500 m3/s) while the Ottawa freshet is high (Apr-Jun) to protect Montreal; otherwise release proportionally to how far the Ontario level is above the 74.7 m target, up to 9,500 m3/s near the 75.5 m flood line, and never drain below the 74.2 m shipping floor. Backtested on 2017 with the actual inflows, the rule caps the summer peak ~0.4 m below the record that flooded shorelines (75.4 vs 75.8 m) and finishes the year ~0.15 m lower on average, with no month approaching the shipping restriction level; cutting releases by 1,000 m3/s (the 2017 actual policy) reproduces the record flooding, showing the flooding was a release decision, not an uncontrollable inflow. Sensitivity: a sustained release error of 500 m3/s moves the annual mean only ~0.15 m, while a 10% inflow forecast error moves it ~0.28 m - so the system is robust to operator error but not to wet years, and the rule's value is bounded, predictable response, not exact tracking. We request acceptance of the model and a 12-month parallel-operation trial against your current policy.'
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Stakeholder constraint set (Lake Ontario): 74.00 <= h <= 75.50 with 74.20-75.00 the normal operating band and 74.70 the target; the controller of task 3 is the pointwise projection of the target onto this set given the flow feasibility. Factor quantification from the 2000-2022 record: Niagara inflow 2000-2022 record mean 6,005 m3/s; 2017 mean 6,808 m3/s (monthly 6,320-7,320), top of the record range; Ottawa freshet 4,467-6,337 m3/s in Apr-May 2017-2018; Ontario level range 74.28-75.91 m across the record, 2017 mean 75.18 m vs record mean 74.83 m. Memo content as stated in the analysis (values above are the memo's numerical claims, each traceable to the task-3 backtest or the task-4 sensitivity runs).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The Ontario focus is justified by the record: 2017 and 2019 are the two highest years in the 23-year window and both exceeded the 75.5 m serious-flood line, while the shipping-side extreme (lowest mean year 74.62 m in 2020-22 levels) never breached 74.20 m inside the window. Data provenance is fully stated: everything numeric in the model and the memo comes from the supplied workbook, the five expert exchanges that fixed the operating parameters, and one literature record for the bathymetry areas - no value was taken from memory. Limitations: the memo's '0.4 m lower peak' claim is the model backtest, not a field trial; the 12-month parallel-operation recommendation is the honest substitute for that. The memo is a summary of tasks 1-4 and adds no new numbers.
tasks.task_description_note: Lake Ontario stakeholder/factor focus, data provenance, and IJC memo.
